Marc Chagall’s Le profil et l’enfant rouge (1960) is a luminous lithograph created during one of the most prolific periods of his career, when he collaborated extensively with the master printer Fernand Mourlot in Paris. This work was included in Chagall Lithographe, Tome I, a landmark volume that helped establish his reputation as one of the greatest modern printmakers. Chagall’s lithographs are celebrated for their dreamlike quality, rich colors, and fusion of personal memory, folklore, and biblical symbolism—often evoking a sense of poetic wonder. With its small edition size and connection to the deluxe publication, this piece exemplifies the technical brilliance and imaginative spirit that made Chagall’s graphic works so influential in 20th-century art.
Hand signed  lower right - "Hypha will cover the world, little by little. 'We should be able to get our hands on that door to the alien world soon. Wait 'til we get there!'"

Takeshi Murakami’s Hypha (2007) reflects his signature blending of contemporary pop culture with traditional Japanese artistic sensibilities, a style often described as “Superflat.” The title references the branching filaments of fungi, which grow and spread invisibly—an idea Murakami has linked to how art and ideas permeate global culture. By the mid-2000s, Murakami was already an international art star, collaborating with major brands like Louis Vuitton and shaping the intersection of fine art and commercial design. Works like Hypha embody both playful surface appeal and deeper commentary on organic growth, globalization, and the interconnectedness of cultural production.

Takashi Murakami’s A Picture of the Blessed Lion Who Stares at Death (2009) is a striking example of his fusion of Buddhist iconography with contemporary pop aesthetics. The lion, a traditional guardian figure in East Asian art and temples, is reimagined through Murakami’s vivid colors and stylized forms, embodying both strength and spiritual transcendence. Created under his Kaikai Kiki studio in Tokyo, the work reflects his practice of producing limited-edition prints that make his art accessible while maintaining high artistic value. This piece also illustrates Murakami’s ongoing dialogue between life, death, and enlightenment, central themes in his body of work that bridge tradition and modernity.

Offset lithograph. Signed and numbered "179/300. Framed
50 x 50 CM - 19 3/4 x 19 3/4 IN. Published by Kaikai Kiki Co., Ltd., Tokyo. Ref.: Kaikai Kiki (2008) Takashi Murakami Prints: “My First Art” Series; Tajan, Paris, 17 Nov 2010, lot 157, ill. p.112.

Takashi Murakami’s And then, when that’s done… (2009) continues his exploration of the iconic “DOB” character, often interpreted as an alter ego and commentary on the commercialization of contemporary culture. Rendered here as an offset lithograph, the work exemplifies Murakami’s “Superflat” aesthetic, merging the slick surfaces of pop art with the layered references of traditional Japanese painting. The character’s wide-eyed, almost manic expression embodies both playful charm and unsettling intensity, reflecting Murakami’s interest in the dualities of innocence and anxiety within modern society. Published by Kaikai Kiki Co., Ltd. in Tokyo and produced in a limited edition of 300, the print underscores Murakami’s commitment to making his art accessible to a broad audience while retaining the exclusivity of fine art production. Exhibited and sold internationally, this piece demonstrates the enduring appeal of Murakami’s visual language, which seamlessly bridges high art, mass media, and global consumer culture.

Käthe Kollwitz was a German artist celebrated for her powerful portrayals of human suffering and resilience. This print (Klipstein 240; Knesebeck 250) is one of her iconic graphic works, noted for its stark emotional intensity and masterful draftsmanship. Kollwitz’s etchings and lithographs remain central to 20th-century German Expressionism.
Signed and numbered 44/100; printed by Mourlot, Paris; published by Salon de Mai, Paris; Mourlot 500; Lot 203

Joan Miró’s Mourlot 500 belongs to his prolific body of color lithographs produced in collaboration with the master printer Fernand Mourlot. This print exemplifies Miró’s signature biomorphic shapes, playful abstraction, and vibrant use of primary colors. Works from the Mourlot series are highly regarded for capturing Miró’s whimsical yet deeply modernist vision.
Pencil-signed and dated lower right; Listing ID 1-B6FKRT / 5198

Robert Rauschenberg’s Foster 34 is part of his innovative printmaking practice, where he combined photographic imagery with experimental processes. A leading figure of post-war American art, Rauschenberg bridged Abstract Expressionism and Pop Art. This edition highlights his interest in layering, collage aesthetics, and the interplay between high art and mass culture.
Signed and numbered 145/249; published by Gruener Janura AG, Glarus & Ugo Meneghini, Venice; printed by Studio Quattro, Venice; Lot 37

Hundertwasser’s Fürst HGW 57 is an example of his vividly colored, organic print editions, filled with spirals, biomorphic forms, and architectural fantasy. Hundertwasser rejected straight lines in favor of nature’s irregularity, and his graphic works embody his ecological and humanist philosophy. This piece reflects his joyful, idiosyncratic visual language.

Woodcut printed from the original 1912 block on thin Japan paper; sheet c.7¾ × 9⅜ in. The print bears Marc’s stylised “M” plus widow’s signature and an estate stamp. Slight uninked horizontal line from a crack in the block; otherwise good. Estimate $7,000–$9,000; current bid $3,500.

Franz Marc’s Schlafende Hirtin (1912) is a rare woodcut from the artist’s groundbreaking Der Blaue Reiter period. With its simplified forms and lyrical symbolism, the print reflects Marc’s search for spiritual harmony between humanity and nature. This impression, authenticated by Maria Marc’s signature and the estate stamp, is characteristic of the very limited editions that survive. A cornerstone of German Expressionist printmaking, it offers collectors a scarce opportunity to acquire a work that embodies both Marc’s artistic vision and the enduring legacy of early modernism.
Etching on paper, pencil‑signed lower right; numbered “XLVIII” (48/??), edition likely <75. Plate ≈ 9.5 × 6.75 in. Great condition with slight wear. Classic British subject.

Sir William Russell Flint’s Slippery Steps exemplifies the artist’s mastery of the etched line and his enduring fascination with atmosphere, elegance, and movement. Executed with exquisite control, the composition captures a fleeting, light-struck moment typical of Flint’s celebrated portrayals of women in intimate European settings. Printed on fine Whatman paper and delicately hand-signed by the artist, this impression conveys the silken tonal transitions and crisp draughtsmanship that define Flint’s best graphic work. Issued in a small numbered edition, Slippery Steps represents Flint’s ability to merge technical precision with poetic grace. For collectors of early-twentieth-century British etching, it stands as both a testament to the artist’s refinement and a touchstone of the “etching revival” that placed Flint among the leading printmakers of his generation.

Screenprint on paper, pencil‑signed and numbered AP 4/15 (edition 15). Image 18.75 × 13.25 in; APs often sought after. Good; minor wear to frame. Extremely low current bid ($5) for a scarce African‑American edition.

Screenprint on paper, pencil-signed lower right, artist’s proof 4/15. Created in 1997, Nathaniel Bustion’s African Girl embodies the artist’s vibrant engagement with identity, rhythm, and cultural memory. Using the layered luminosity of the screenprint medium, Bustion distills his subject into bold planes of color and sculptural contour, evoking both modernist abstraction and the visual cadences of African art. The poised figure—at once iconic and intimate—reflects Bustion’s lifelong exploration of Black womanhood and the strength and dignity of everyday experience. Printed in a rare artist’s proof edition of only fifteen impressions, this work demonstrates the meticulous craft and expressive power that define Bustion’s late-twentieth-century practice. With its dynamic balance of form and hue, African Girl stands as a compelling testament to the artist’s vision—bridging modern printmaking technique and the affirming spirit of the African diaspora in contemporary American art.
Zu Kurt Schwitters: La Loterie du Jardin Zoologique

Artist: Max Ernst (1891–1976). Medium: Etching with hand-coloring on paper. Signature: Pencil-signed lower right (“Max Ernst”). Edition: 2/12. Printer: Georges Visat. Publisher: Librairie Les Pas Perdus, Paris. Date: Circa 1951. Image size: 4.75 × 3.5 in (12 × 9 cm) Framed size: 14 × 11.75 in. Condition: Excellent, with light age wear. See Full Report Here.

Max Ernst’s Zu: Kurt Schwitters, La Loterie du Jardin Zoologique (1951) is a rare etching with hand-coloring from a deluxe edition of only twelve impressions, printed by Georges Visat in Paris and published by Librairie Les Pas Perdus. The work pays homage to Ernst’s fellow Dadaist Kurt Schwitters, merging playful surrealist chance imagery with precise intaglio technique. Each impression was individually hand-colored, resulting in subtle variations and making every sheet unique. This impression, numbered 2/12, bears full provenance from its first recorded sale at Butterfield & Butterfield in 1998 to its subsequent offering at Bradford’s Auction Gallery in 2025.

Artist: Käthe Kollwitz (1867–1945). Medium: Etching and aquatint in sepia on wove paper. Signature: Pencil-signed lower right (“Käthe Kollwitz”); plate-signed lower right within image. Edition: From the edition of 30, published circa 1920 by Emil Richter, Dresden. Catalogue Raisonné: Klipstein 122 (VII state). Image size: 5.5 × 3.9 in (14 × 9.9 cm); sheet 12.8 × 9.6 in (32.5 × 24.5 cm). Provenance: Private Collection, Westmount QC → Waddington’s, Toronto (11 Apr 2019, Lot 175) → Private Collection, Toronto ON → Waddington’s Editions Sale (30 Oct 2025, Lot 14). Condition: Very good overall; minor surface accretions in upper-left and lower-right margins only. Notes: A finely printed, lifetime Richter-edition impression showing warm plate tone and full margins. See Full Report Here.

Käthe Kollwitz’s Selbstbildnis (1912) is one of the artist’s most intimate and widely recognized etched self-portraits, executed at the height of her mature period. Printed in sepia aquatint and etching, this striking image belongs to the scarce Emil Richter edition of thirty impressions issued circa 1920. Each was hand-signed by Kollwitz, reflecting her personal oversight of the printing. The work demonstrates her masterful balance of strength and vulnerability through densely hatched lines and luminous chiaroscuro. This impression bears full, untrimmed margins and rich plate tone characteristic of early pulls. Its provenance traces from a private collection in Westmount, Quebec, to Waddington’s (Toronto) in 2019 and again in 2025, confirming a continuous and well-documented ownership history.

On wove paper. Pencil-signed and titled in the lower margin; red jizuri (self-printed) seal in left margin. Edition: Lifetime edition printed under the artist’s supervision; Abe Catalogue #094. Notes: Richly inked impression with brilliant gold-mica background and delicate color transitions in the flesh tones—an outstanding example of Yoshida’s technical refinement.

Hiroshi Yoshida’s Study of a Nude (Shūsaku) (1927) is among the artist’s rare Western-style figure studies, revealing his fusion of Japanese woodblock technique with European realism. Printed in subtle gradations of rose, ochre, and gold, the work exemplifies Yoshida’s technical brilliance and sensitivity to human form. Each lifetime impression bears the artist’s pencil signature, title, and the red jizuri (self-printed) seal—attesting that the print was pulled under Yoshida’s direct supervision at his Tokyo workshop. The present sheet, noted for its luminous mica background and well-preserved color balance, descends from a Toronto private collection and was acquired at Waddington’s Editions Sale (October 2025). Comparable impressions have achieved strong results at Mainichi Auction (Tokyo) and Bonhams (London), underscoring its desirability among collectors of early modern Japanese printmaking.

This offset lithograph belongs to Takashi Murakami’s celebrated “And Then” series, characterized by immersive and hypnotic chromatic intensity. Dominated by a deep ultramarine ground, the composition is animated by subtle variations in color—particularly in the eyes and facial elements—giving each impression a distinctive visual rhythm despite its serial format. Murakami’s offset prints are produced through highly controlled, multi-stage processes that achieve exceptional sharpness, saturation, and surface complexity. For collectors, the work is especially appealing as a refined example of Murakami’s print practice, combining technical sophistication, visual richness, and the quiet uniqueness that distinguishes individual impressions within this iconic series.

Serigraph in color on paper, signed by the artist in pen (faded) lower right. Image depicts a dynamic nautical scene with bold movement and vivid blues. Sheet measures approximately 25 3/4 × 18 1/4 in. Signed in pen lower right — signature is somewhat faded but still legible.

LeRoy Neiman (American, 1921–2012) is known for his energetic, expressionistic style and vibrant portrayals of sports, entertainment, and leisure culture. “High Sea Sailings” showcases Neiman’s layered color approach and active mark-making, capturing both motion and atmosphere. This vibrant serigraph exemplifies LeRoy Neiman’s dynamic approach to movement, color, and spectacle, hallmarks of his celebrated late-career work. Known internationally for his depictions of major sporting and leisure events, Neiman captures the exhilaration of open-water sailing through energetic mark-making and saturated hues. Created in 1995, the print reflects the artist’s mature mastery of the serigraph medium, which allowed him to translate the spontaneity of his painting into richly layered color. For collectors, High Sea Sailings is especially appealing as a strong, recognizable example of Neiman’s iconic style, combining visual immediacy with the enduring popularity of his nautical and sports imagery in the secondary market.
Delteil 3; fine proof printed in brown on thin ivory vellum; small normal margins

This etching exemplifies Jean-François Millet’s radical elevation of rural labor to a subject of moral and artistic gravity, a vision that profoundly influenced later realists and modernists, including Van Gogh. The solitary figure—caught between effort and repose—embodies Millet’s belief in the quiet heroism of peasant life, rendered through an economy of line that gives the image unusual emotional force. Created during the height of the Barbizon movement, the work reflects Millet’s direct engagement with agricultural life around Barbizon rather than academic idealization. For collectors, Millet’s etchings are especially appealing for their rarity relative to his paintings and for offering a direct, intimate expression of the ideas that shaped nineteenth-century social realism.
Guérin 291; very fine proof on Montval laid paper; signed with monogram in pencil; full margins; dry stamp H. Petiet

This lithograph reflects Aristide Maillol’s classical approach to the female form, emphasizing harmony, weight, and sculptural calm. The seated nude, partially enveloped in drapery, is rendered with simplified contours and balanced proportions that echo Maillol’s work as a sculptor. Rejecting expressive excess, the composition conveys a timeless serenity rooted in classical tradition. The print exemplifies Maillol’s pursuit of idealized form and quiet monumentality in modern art. Presenting Sculptural serenity over anecdote or symbolism. Closely aligned with his work in stone and bronze, the composition demonstrates Maillol’s conviction that modern art could renew classical ideals through simplification and restraint. Unlike many printmakers, Maillol treated graphic works as extensions of his sculptural practice, giving his prints a distinctive sense of volume and permanence. Collectors value Maillol’s lithographs for their clarity of form and for providing access to the artist’s core aesthetic at a scale and intimacy unavailable in his monumental sculpture.
Ginestet & Pouillon 670; very fine proof on vellum; numbered and signed in pencil by Picasso; mounted on cardboard; edition of 200; Bernheim-Jeune

Maternity reflects Picasso’s sustained engagement with themes of motherhood and tenderness during a pivotal period shaped by his relationship with Marie-Thérèse Walter. Executed in etching and aquatint with delicate color, the work demonstrates Picasso’s belief that printmaking could rival painting in emotional subtlety and formal invention. Images of maternity recur throughout his career, but works from this period are especially admired for their lyrical calm and classical balance. For collectors, the print offers a compelling combination of intimacy, technical sophistication, and a central theme within Picasso’s broader oeuvre. Maternity belongs to Picasso’s profound exploration of motherhood and familial intimacy during the late 1920s and early 1930s, a period shaped by his relationship with Marie-Thérèse Walter. Executed in etching and aquatint with subtle color, the work demonstrates Picasso’s mastery of printmaking as an expressive medium equal to painting. Images of maternity recur throughout Picasso’s career, but works from this period are particularly prized for their tenderness and classical calm. The composition bridges modern abstraction and ancient archetype, reinforcing Picasso’s ability to renew timeless themes through radical economy of form.
Bloch 77; Baer II 8; very fine proof on strong white vellum; numbered and signed in brush and sepia ink; edition of 250; provenance: Ambroise Vollard → Henri Marie Petiet

This etching forms part of Picasso’s celebrated Vollard Suite, widely regarded as one of the most important published print series of the twentieth century. Created during a period of intense personal and artistic experimentation, the composition explores intimacy and psychological tension through confident, economical line. The Vollard Suite marked Picasso’s full command of etching as a primary creative language, rather than a secondary medium. Collectors prize works from the suite for their art-historical importance, strong market demand, and for offering direct insight into Picasso’s evolving themes of desire, power, and human connection.
J. Arthur, Richard Estes: Painting and Prints, Pomegranate Artbooks, 1993, pp. 125–126

Screenprint from 1982 depicting the iconic British comic-strip character Andy Capp, rendered through Estes’s crisp photorealist sensibility. Published during a period when Estes was extending his vocabulary beyond urban storefronts into popular imagery, the print balances graphic clarity with subtle spatial depth. Literature reference: J. Arthur, Richard Estes: Painting and Prints, Pomegranate Artbooks, 1993, pp. 125–126.

Richard Estes’s Andy Capp (1982) offers a rare intersection between American photorealism and popular culture. Best known for his meticulously observed cityscapes, Estes here applies the same precision and compositional control to a universally recognizable comic figure. The result is both playful and formally rigorous, underscoring Estes’s ability to elevate mass-media imagery through refined printmaking technique. Works from this period are sought after for demonstrating the breadth of Estes’s practice beyond architectural subjects, appealing to collectors of both Pop-inflected and photorealist prints.

Lithograph from 1925 depicting a seated female reader holding a bouquet of roses. Catalogued as Duthuit 471. The composition exemplifies Matisse’s early mastery of line and contour, combining interior calm with decorative balance. Executed during a formative decade in which Matisse refined his graphic language alongside painting and sculpture.

Liseuse au Bouquet de Roses (1925) is a lyrical example of Henri Matisse’s graphic work from the interwar period, when his lithographs became an essential extension of his artistic vision. With economy of line and a serene, intimate subject, the print reflects Matisse’s lifelong pursuit of harmony, balance, and expressive simplicity. Works from this era are particularly prized for their clarity and elegance, offering collectors direct insight into Matisse’s approach to form and rhythm. The image’s quiet intimacy and strong art-historical placement make it a highly desirable early Matisse lithograph.

Pierre Bonnard — Portrait of Renoir (1916). Very fine proof on Arches vellum, printed by Fort for Vollard; edition of 150 copies. Catalog reference: Bouvet 84. Deluxe Vollard-era impression with full margins and pronounced plate tone; typical Bonnard warmth and subtle handling of line.

Pierre Bonnard — *Portrait of Renoir* (1916). A refined Bonnard proof executed with the artist’s characteristic intimacy: the etching’s delicate line and warm plate tone capture Renoir’s gentle modeling and the painterly tactility Bonnard brought to graphic work. Printed on **Arches vellum** by Fort for Vollard (edition **150**, Bouvet 84), this proof presents the deluxe qualities collectors prize in the Vollard publications — generous margins, strong plate presence, and a tactile surface that reads like a small-scale painting. As a portrait of a close contemporary and fellow artist, the sheet has both biographical resonance and market desirability for connoisseurs of early-20th-century French printmaking.

Félix Buhot — The Crossing (1879). Superb proof on old laid paper, definitive state (multi-technique: etching, drypoint and roulette). Catalog note: stamped, signed and annotated in pencil by the artist “Essai tiré à 35 épreuves” — an annotated trial impression of particular rarity.

Félix Buhot — *The Crossing* (1879). Buhot’s multi-technique approach — etching, drypoint and roulette — is on full display in this superb proof, which conveys nocturnal atmosphere through layered biting and rouletted textures. The lot text records an artist-annotated trial impression (“**Essai tiré à 35 épreuves**”), a status that enhances rarity and scholarly interest: such annotated proofs offer direct evidence of the artist’s working method and the developmental sequence of the plate. Collectors prize Buhot for the tactile complexity and tonal subtlety of his fin-de-siècle Parisian scenes, and this proof is a particularly strong example.

Henri-Edmond Cross — La Promenade (The Cypresses) (1897). Very fine proof on chine appliqué to heavyweight vellum, signed and numbered in pencil; edition 100 proofs for the Album d’estampes originales de la Galerie Vollard (Johnson 27). Full margins; minor tiny breaks and slight yellowing in large margins noted.

Henri-Edmond Cross — *La Promenade (The Cypresses)* (1897). A deluxe impression from the Vollard album, here offered as a very fine proof **on chine appliqué to heavyweight vellum**, signed and numbered (edition **100**, Johnson 27). The sheet demonstrates Cross’s mature color lithograph technique: luminous planar color, subtle modulation of hue, and a lyrical, post-Impressionist sense of rhythm. Condition notes indicate tiny breaks and very slight yellowing in the margins, but the print retains the chromatic refinement and rarefied surface collectors seek among Provençal-period color lithographs.

Henri-Edmond Cross — At the Champs-Élysées (1898). Very fine proof on chine appliqué to japon, stamped and numbered in pencil. Deluxe proof from the deluxe issue (edition 75); full margins and strong colour-printing quality as described by the house.

Henri-Edmond Cross — *At the Champs-Élysées* (1898). This deluxe proof on **chine appliqué to japon** belongs to the uncommon deluxe issue (edition **75**) and is stamped and numbered in pencil. The work exemplifies Cross’s translation of pointillist color into the lithographic medium — crisp, orchestrated color planes and a decorative sense of urban spectacle. Deluxe proofs from this series are desirable for the rarity of the state and the exceptional print quality they exhibit.

Eugène Delacroix — Arabs of Oran (1833). Superb and rare proof on Hollande laid paper (watermark: Aquafortists), described as the 1st state (of 6) with the title in-point and before the letter/bevels; edition of 50. Very desirable early-state Delacroix impression with full margins.

Eugène Delacroix — *Arabs of Oran* (1833). An important early-state impression: a superb proof on **Hollande laid paper** (Aquafortists watermark), recorded as the **1st state (of 6)** with title in-point and before letter/bevels (edition **50**). The subject sits within Delacroix’s orientalist repertoire, and an early state of this plate offers both art-historical significance and rarity: early states often reveal compositional decisions and plate development that scholars and collectors prize, while the Holland paper and full margins mark it as a desirable collector’s example.
Dios se lo pague a usted (God gives it back to you)

Francisco de Goya — Dios se lo pague a usted (God gives it back to you). Superb proof before the letter, on Holland paper with large margins; from the first edition (1867). Catalog reference: Delteil 24. The sale notes only two early proofs known — a significant early-state example.

Francisco de Goya — *Dios se lo pague a usted (God gives it back to you).* A superb **proof before the letter**, on Holland paper with large margins, cited to the first edition (1867) and catalogued **Delteil 24**. The house notes only two early proofs known in this state, making it an exceptionally rare early impression. Such proofs are crucial for understanding Goya’s plate states and for collectors who prioritize lifetime impressions and important early issues of his etchings.

Francisco de Goya — Mejor es holgar (Caprice 73). Very fine proof on cream vellum printed in bistre, before the copper bevels of the second edition (1850). Catalog reference: Delteil 110. Early/impression-quality proof with strong contrast and plate detail.

Francisco de Goya — *Mejor es holgar (Caprice 73).* A very fine proof **on cream vellum** printed in bistre and recorded **before the bevels** of the second edition (1850); cited as **Delteil 110**. As a caprice, the sheet belongs to Goya’s central project of social satire and moral observation; early/impression-quality proofs such as this one are valued for technical clarity and for their testimony to the artist’s print practice across editions and states.

Alexandre Lunois — A bullfight in the countryside (plate 8, La Corrida). Plate 8 of the La Corrida suite; very fine proof on chine, signed with printer/publisher noted as G. Pellet éditeur. Condition note: small angular tear. Ferri notes an edition of 100 (including ≈25 with remarks); the raisonné (Édouard André, p.221) records the series and the plate — “Tirage de chaque planche: 50 épreuves.”

Alexandre Lunois — *A bullfight in the countryside* (plate 8, *La Corrida*). Plate **8** of the *La Corrida* suite — a color lithograph executed with the pastel-like sensibility Lunois applied to Spanish subjects. The Ferri text records a **very fine proof on chine**, signed and published by **G. Pellet**, and notes a **small angular tear**; Ferri cites an edition of 100 (with a subset of impressions “with remarks”), while Édouard André’s raisonné (*Alexandre Lunois*, H. Floury, 1914, p.221) documents the suite and records *“Tirage de chaque planche: 50 épreuves.”* The plate embodies Lunois’s fluency for spectacle and chromatic nuance — the bullfight suite is prized for its lively crowd scenes, vigorous pastel character, and its place within early-20th-century Franco-Spanish lithography.

Édouard Manet — Olympia (large plate). Very rare early-state etching on Van der Ley laid paper (watermark), described as a very early state with the first signature; the lower square line is only faintly indicated and the background is unfinished — provenance to Ph. Burty is recorded. Catalog note stresses extreme rarity (two proofs mentioned).

Édouard Manet — *Olympia (large plate).* A very rare **early-state etching** on **Van der Ley laid paper** with provenance to **Ph. Burty**; the catalog highlights an unusual state with a first signature and a faintly indicated lower square line, leaving background areas less worked — a document of Manet’s process. Early proofs of *Olympia* are among the most coveted Manet graphic rarities because they illuminate the artist’s handling of composition and figure; this large-plate early state has exceptional art-historical resonance and strong market interest.

Jean-François Millet — La Précaution maternelle (1862). Very fine trial proof (original glass plate noted in the sale); Sagot edition of 150; stamped and annotated by the editor on the verso. Rare trial impression with strong tonal modelling; catalog reference Delteil 27.

Jean-François Millet — *La Précaution maternelle* (1862). Presented as a very fine **trial proof** (glass-plate trial noted), from the Sagot edition of **150**, stamped and annotated on the verso by the editor; cited **Delteil 27**. Millet’s subject — maternal care and rural life — is expressed here with intimate tonal modeling and an economy of line; trial proofs of such plates are particularly prized for their immediacy and for revealing the artist’s working decisions prior to the standardized edition.

Marc Chagall’s Le profil et l’enfant rouge (1960) is a luminous lithograph created during one of the most prolific periods of his career, when he collaborated extensively with the master printer Fernand Mourlot in Paris. This work was included in Chagall Lithographe, Tome I, a landmark volume that helped establish his reputation as one of the greatest modern printmakers. Chagall’s lithographs are celebrated for their dreamlike quality, rich colors, and fusion of personal memory, folklore, and biblical symbolism—often evoking a sense of poetic wonder. With its small edition size and connection to the deluxe publication, this piece exemplifies the technical brilliance and imaginative spirit that made Chagall’s graphic works so influential in 20th-century art.

Takeshi Murakami’s Hypha (2007) reflects his signature blending of contemporary pop culture with traditional Japanese artistic sensibilities, a style often described as “Superflat.” The title references the branching filaments of fungi, which grow and spread invisibly—an idea Murakami has linked to how art and ideas permeate global culture. By the mid-2000s, Murakami was already an international art star, collaborating with major brands like Louis Vuitton and shaping the intersection of fine art and commercial design. Works like Hypha embody both playful surface appeal and deeper commentary on organic growth, globalization, and the interconnectedness of cultural production.

Takashi Murakami’s A Picture of the Blessed Lion Who Stares at Death (2009) is a striking example of his fusion of Buddhist iconography with contemporary pop aesthetics. The lion, a traditional guardian figure in East Asian art and temples, is reimagined through Murakami’s vivid colors and stylized forms, embodying both strength and spiritual transcendence. Created under his Kaikai Kiki studio in Tokyo, the work reflects his practice of producing limited-edition prints that make his art accessible while maintaining high artistic value. This piece also illustrates Murakami’s ongoing dialogue between life, death, and enlightenment, central themes in his body of work that bridge tradition and modernity.

Takashi Murakami’s And then, when that’s done… (2009) continues his exploration of the iconic “DOB” character, often interpreted as an alter ego and commentary on the commercialization of contemporary culture. Rendered here as an offset lithograph, the work exemplifies Murakami’s “Superflat” aesthetic, merging the slick surfaces of pop art with the layered references of traditional Japanese painting. The character’s wide-eyed, almost manic expression embodies both playful charm and unsettling intensity, reflecting Murakami’s interest in the dualities of innocence and anxiety within modern society. Published by Kaikai Kiki Co., Ltd. in Tokyo and produced in a limited edition of 300, the print underscores Murakami’s commitment to making his art accessible to a broad audience while retaining the exclusivity of fine art production. Exhibited and sold internationally, this piece demonstrates the enduring appeal of Murakami’s visual language, which seamlessly bridges high art, mass media, and global consumer culture.

Hundertwasser rejected straight lines in favor of nature’s irregularity, and his graphic works embody his ecological and humanist philosophy. LeRoy Neiman (American, 1921–2012) is known for his energetic, expressionistic style and vibrant portrayals of sports, entertainment, and leisure culture. “High Sea Sailings” showcases Neiman’s layered color approach and active mark-making, capturing both motion and atmosphere. This vibrant serigraph exemplifies LeRoy Neiman’s dynamic approach to movement, color, and spectacle, hallmarks of his celebrated late-career work. Known internationally for his depictions of major sporting and leisure events, Neiman captures the exhilaration of open-water sailing through energetic mark-making and saturated hues. Created in 1995, the print reflects the artist’s mature mastery of the serigraph medium, which allowed him to translate the spontaneity of his painting into richly layered color. For collectors, High Sea Sailings is especially appealing as a strong, recognizable example of Neiman’s iconic style, combining visual immediacy with the enduring popularity of his nautical and sports imagery in the secondary market.

This etching exemplifies Jean-François Millet’s radical elevation of rural labor to a subject of moral and artistic gravity, a vision that profoundly influenced later realists and modernists, including Van Gogh. The solitary figure—caught between effort and repose—embodies Millet’s belief in the quiet heroism of peasant life, rendered through an economy of line that gives the image unusual emotional force. Created during the height of the Barbizon movement, the work reflects Millet’s direct engagement with agricultural life around Barbizon rather than academic idealization. For collectors, Millet’s etchings are especially appealing for their rarity relative to his paintings and for offering a direct, intimate expression of the ideas that shaped nineteenth-century social realism.

This lithograph reflects Aristide Maillol’s classical approach to the female form, emphasizing harmony, weight, and sculptural calm. The seated nude, partially enveloped in drapery, is rendered with simplified contours and balanced proportions that echo Maillol’s work as a sculptor. Rejecting expressive excess, the composition conveys a timeless serenity rooted in classical tradition. The print exemplifies Maillol’s pursuit of idealized form and quiet monumentality in modern art. Presenting Sculptural serenity over anecdote or symbolism. Closely aligned with his work in stone and bronze, the composition demonstrates Maillol’s conviction that modern art could renew classical ideals through simplification and restraint. Unlike many printmakers, Maillol treated graphic works as extensions of his sculptural practice, giving his prints a distinctive sense of volume and permanence. Collectors value Maillol’s lithographs for their clarity of form and for providing access to the artist’s core aesthetic at a scale and intimacy unavailable in his monumental sculpture.

Maternity reflects Picasso’s sustained engagement with themes of motherhood and tenderness during a pivotal period shaped by his relationship with Marie-Thérèse Walter. Executed in etching and aquatint with delicate color, the work demonstrates Picasso’s belief that printmaking could rival painting in emotional subtlety and formal invention. Images of maternity recur throughout his career, but works from this period are especially admired for their lyrical calm and classical balance. For collectors, the print offers a compelling combination of intimacy, technical sophistication, and a central theme within Picasso’s broader oeuvre. Maternity belongs to Picasso’s profound exploration of motherhood and familial intimacy during the late 1920s and early 1930s, a period shaped by his relationship with Marie-Thérèse Walter. Executed in etching and aquatint with subtle color, the work demonstrates Picasso’s mastery of printmaking as an expressive medium equal to painting. Images of maternity recur throughout Picasso’s career, but works from this period are particularly prized for their tenderness and classical calm. The composition bridges modern abstraction and ancient archetype, reinforcing Picasso’s ability to renew timeless themes through radical economy of form.

This etching forms part of Picasso’s celebrated Vollard Suite, widely regarded as one of the most important published print series of the twentieth century. Created during a period of intense personal and artistic experimentation, the composition explores intimacy and psychological tension through confident, economical line. The Vollard Suite marked Picasso’s full command of etching as a primary creative language, rather than a secondary medium. Collectors prize works from the suite for their art-historical importance, strong market demand, and for offering direct insight into Picasso’s evolving themes of desire, power, and human connection.

Richard Estes’s Andy Capp (1982) offers a rare intersection between American photorealism and popular culture. Best known for his meticulously observed cityscapes, Estes here applies the same precision and compositional control to a universally recognizable comic figure. The result is both playful and formally rigorous, underscoring Estes’s ability to elevate mass-media imagery through refined printmaking technique. Works from this period are sought after for demonstrating the breadth of Estes’s practice beyond architectural subjects, appealing to collectors of both Pop-inflected and photorealist prints.

Liseuse au Bouquet de Roses (1925) is a lyrical example of Henri Matisse’s graphic work from the interwar period, when his lithographs became an essential extension of his artistic vision. With economy of line and a serene, intimate subject, the print reflects Matisse’s lifelong pursuit of harmony, balance, and expressive simplicity. Works from this era are particularly prized for their clarity and elegance, offering collectors direct insight into Matisse’s approach to form and rhythm. The image’s quiet intimacy and strong art-historical placement make it a highly desirable early Matisse lithograph.

Pierre Bonnard — *Portrait of Renoir* (1916). Collectors prize Buhot for the tactile complexity and tonal subtlety of his fin-de-siècle Parisian scenes, and this proof is a particularly strong example.

Marc Chagall’s Le profil et l’enfant rouge (1960) is a luminous lithograph created during one of the most prolific periods of his career, when he collaborated extensively with the master printer Fernand Mourlot in Paris. This work was included in Chagall Lithographe, Tome I, a landmark volume that helped establish his reputation as one of the greatest modern printmakers. Chagall’s lithographs are celebrated for their dreamlike quality, rich colors, and fusion of personal memory, folklore, and biblical symbolism—often evoking a sense of poetic wonder. With its small edition size and connection to the deluxe publication, this piece exemplifies the technical brilliance and imaginative spirit that made Chagall’s graphic works so influential in 20th-century art.

Takeshi Murakami’s Hypha (2007) reflects his signature blending of contemporary pop culture with traditional Japanese artistic sensibilities, a style often described as “Superflat.” The title references the branching filaments of fungi, which grow and spread invisibly—an idea Murakami has linked to how art and ideas permeate global culture. By the mid-2000s, Murakami was already an international art star, collaborating with major brands like Louis Vuitton and shaping the intersection of fine art and commercial design. Works like Hypha embody both playful surface appeal and deeper commentary on organic growth, globalization, and the interconnectedness of cultural production.

Takashi Murakami’s A Picture of the Blessed Lion Who Stares at Death (2009) is a striking example of his fusion of Buddhist iconography with contemporary pop aesthetics. The lion, a traditional guardian figure in East Asian art and temples, is reimagined through Murakami’s vivid colors and stylized forms, embodying both strength and spiritual transcendence. Created under his Kaikai Kiki studio in Tokyo, the work reflects his practice of producing limited-edition prints that make his art accessible while maintaining high artistic value. This piece also illustrates Murakami’s ongoing dialogue between life, death, and enlightenment, central themes in his body of work that bridge tradition and modernity.

Takashi Murakami’s And then, when that’s done… (2009) continues his exploration of the iconic “DOB” character, often interpreted as an alter ego and commentary on the commercialization of contemporary culture. Rendered here as an offset lithograph, the work exemplifies Murakami’s “Superflat” aesthetic, merging the slick surfaces of pop art with the layered references of traditional Japanese painting. The character’s wide-eyed, almost manic expression embodies both playful charm and unsettling intensity, reflecting Murakami’s interest in the dualities of innocence and anxiety within modern society. Published by Kaikai Kiki Co., Ltd. in Tokyo and produced in a limited edition of 300, the print underscores Murakami’s commitment to making his art accessible to a broad audience while retaining the exclusivity of fine art production. Exhibited and sold internationally, this piece demonstrates the enduring appeal of Murakami’s visual language, which seamlessly bridges high art, mass media, and global consumer culture.

This etching exemplifies Jean-François Millet’s radical elevation of rural labor to a subject of moral and artistic gravity, a vision that profoundly influenced later realists and modernists, including Van Gogh. The solitary figure—caught between effort and repose—embodies Millet’s belief in the quiet heroism of peasant life, rendered through an economy of line that gives the image unusual emotional force. Created during the height of the Barbizon movement, the work reflects Millet’s direct engagement with agricultural life around Barbizon rather than academic idealization. For collectors, Millet’s etchings are especially appealing for their rarity relative to his paintings and for offering a direct, intimate expression of the ideas that shaped nineteenth-century social realism.

This lithograph reflects Aristide Maillol’s classical approach to the female form, emphasizing harmony, weight, and sculptural calm. The seated nude, partially enveloped in drapery, is rendered with simplified contours and balanced proportions that echo Maillol’s work as a sculptor. Rejecting expressive excess, the composition conveys a timeless serenity rooted in classical tradition. The print exemplifies Maillol’s pursuit of idealized form and quiet monumentality in modern art. Presenting Sculptural serenity over anecdote or symbolism. Closely aligned with his work in stone and bronze, the composition demonstrates Maillol’s conviction that modern art could renew classical ideals through simplification and restraint. Unlike many printmakers, Maillol treated graphic works as extensions of his sculptural practice, giving his prints a distinctive sense of volume and permanence. Collectors value Maillol’s lithographs for their clarity of form and for providing access to the artist’s core aesthetic at a scale and intimacy unavailable in his monumental sculpture.

Images of maternity recur throughout Picasso’s career, but works from this period are particularly prized for their tenderness and classical calm. Collectors prize works from the suite for their art-historical importance, strong market demand, and for offering direct insight into Picasso’s evolving themes of desire, power, and human connection.

Richard Estes’s Andy Capp (1982) offers a rare intersection between American photorealism and popular culture. Works from this period are sought after for demonstrating the breadth of Estes’s practice beyond architectural subjects, appealing to collectors of both Pop-inflected and photorealist prints.

With economy of line and a serene, intimate subject, the print reflects Matisse’s lifelong pursuit of harmony, balance, and expressive simplicity. Works from this era are particularly prized for their clarity and elegance, offering collectors direct insight into Matisse’s approach to form and rhythm. The image’s quiet intimacy and strong art-historical placement make it a highly desirable early Matisse lithograph.

Pierre Bonnard — Portrait of Renoir (1916). Very fine proof on Arches vellum, printed by Fort for Vollard; edition of 150 copies. Catalog reference: Bouvet 84. Deluxe Vollard-era impression with full margins and pronounced plate tone; typical Bonnard warmth and subtle handling of line.

Pierre Bonnard — *Portrait of Renoir* (1916). A refined Bonnard proof executed with the artist’s characteristic intimacy: the etching’s delicate line and warm plate tone capture Renoir’s gentle modeling and the painterly tactility Bonnard brought to graphic work. Printed on **Arches vellum** by Fort for Vollard (edition **150**, Bouvet 84), this proof presents the deluxe qualities collectors prize in the Vollard publications — generous margins, strong plate presence, and a tactile surface that reads like a small-scale painting. As a portrait of a close contemporary and fellow artist, the sheet has both biographical resonance and market desirability for connoisseurs of early-20th-century French printmaking.

Félix Buhot — The Crossing (1879). Superb proof on old laid paper, definitive state (multi-technique: etching, drypoint and roulette). Catalog note: stamped, signed and annotated in pencil by the artist “Essai tiré à 35 épreuves” — an annotated trial impression of particular rarity.

Félix Buhot — *The Crossing* (1879). Buhot’s multi-technique approach — etching, drypoint and roulette — is on full display in this superb proof, which conveys nocturnal atmosphere through layered biting and rouletted textures. The lot text records an artist-annotated trial impression (“**Essai tiré à 35 épreuves**”), a status that enhances rarity and scholarly interest: such annotated proofs offer direct evidence of the artist’s working method and the developmental sequence of the plate. Collectors prize Buhot for the tactile complexity and tonal subtlety of his fin-de-siècle Parisian scenes, and this proof is a particularly strong example.

Henri-Edmond Cross — La Promenade (The Cypresses) (1897). Very fine proof on chine appliqué to heavyweight vellum, signed and numbered in pencil; edition 100 proofs for the Album d’estampes originales de la Galerie Vollard (Johnson 27). Full margins; minor tiny breaks and slight yellowing in large margins noted.

Henri-Edmond Cross — *La Promenade (The Cypresses)* (1897). A deluxe impression from the Vollard album, here offered as a very fine proof **on chine appliqué to heavyweight vellum**, signed and numbered (edition **100**, Johnson 27). The sheet demonstrates Cross’s mature color lithograph technique: luminous planar color, subtle modulation of hue, and a lyrical, post-Impressionist sense of rhythm. Condition notes indicate tiny breaks and very slight yellowing in the margins, but the print retains the chromatic refinement and rarefied surface collectors seek among Provençal-period color lithographs.

Henri-Edmond Cross — At the Champs-Élysées (1898). Very fine proof on chine appliqué to japon, stamped and numbered in pencil. Deluxe proof from the deluxe issue (edition 75); full margins and strong colour-printing quality as described by the house.

Henri-Edmond Cross — *At the Champs-Élysées* (1898). This deluxe proof on **chine appliqué to japon** belongs to the uncommon deluxe issue (edition **75**) and is stamped and numbered in pencil. The work exemplifies Cross’s translation of pointillist color into the lithographic medium — crisp, orchestrated color planes and a decorative sense of urban spectacle. Deluxe proofs from this series are desirable for the rarity of the state and the exceptional print quality they exhibit.

Eugène Delacroix — Arabs of Oran (1833). Superb and rare proof on Hollande laid paper (watermark: Aquafortists), described as the 1st state (of 6) with the title in-point and before the letter/bevels; edition of 50. Very desirable early-state Delacroix impression with full margins.

Eugène Delacroix — *Arabs of Oran* (1833). An important early-state impression: a superb proof on **Hollande laid paper** (Aquafortists watermark), recorded as the **1st state (of 6)** with title in-point and before letter/bevels (edition **50**). The subject sits within Delacroix’s orientalist repertoire, and an early state of this plate offers both art-historical significance and rarity: early states often reveal compositional decisions and plate development that scholars and collectors prize, while the Holland paper and full margins mark it as a desirable collector’s example.

Francisco de Goya — Dios se lo pague a usted (God gives it back to you). Superb proof before the letter, on Holland paper with large margins; from the first edition (1867). Catalog reference: Delteil 24. The sale notes only two early proofs known — a significant early-state example.

Francisco de Goya — *Dios se lo pague a usted (God gives it back to you).* A superb **proof before the letter**, on Holland paper with large margins, cited to the first edition (1867) and catalogued **Delteil 24**. The house notes only two early proofs known in this state, making it an exceptionally rare early impression. Such proofs are crucial for understanding Goya’s plate states and for collectors who prioritize lifetime impressions and important early issues of his etchings.

Francisco de Goya — Mejor es holgar (Caprice 73). Very fine proof on cream vellum printed in bistre, before the copper bevels of the second edition (1850). Catalog reference: Delteil 110. Early/impression-quality proof with strong contrast and plate detail.

Francisco de Goya — *Mejor es holgar (Caprice 73).* A very fine proof **on cream vellum** printed in bistre and recorded **before the bevels** of the second edition (1850); cited as **Delteil 110**. As a caprice, the sheet belongs to Goya’s central project of social satire and moral observation; early/impression-quality proofs such as this one are valued for technical clarity and for their testimony to the artist’s print practice across editions and states.

Alexandre Lunois — *A bullfight in the countryside* (plate 8, *La Corrida*). The Ferri text records a **very fine proof on chine**, signed and published by **G. Édouard Manet — *Olympia (large plate).* A very rare **early-state etching** on **Van der Ley laid paper** with provenance to **Ph. Early proofs of *Olympia* are among the most coveted Manet graphic rarities because they illuminate the artist’s handling of composition and figure; this large-plate early state has exceptional art-historical resonance and strong market interest.

Bernard Naudin — Le Concerto (set of 3) (1924). Bernard Naudin — *Le Concerto* (set of 3) (1924). Offered as a mixed media ensemble — an **original ink drawing (Indian ink wash with ochre highlights)**, signed and dated, combined with companion prints — this lot preserves the dialog between the artist’s hand-drawn study and its printed counterparts. Naudin’s engraving and etching practice often explores social and musical themes with rhythmic line and tonal washes; collectors prize sets that include an original drawing alongside printed variants for provenance, artistic process, and display flexibility.

Pablo Picasso — The Monkey (1936). Original etching with aquatint and drypoint (Plate 12 from the Eaux-fortes originales for Buffon). Pablo Picasso — *The Monkey* (1936). The sheet represents Picasso’s mastery of intaglio techniques during the 1930s — combining line, tonal aquatint, and a painterly sense of black — and signed, vellum proofs of this plate are highly sought for their technical distinction and direct connection to the artist’s workshop practice.

Félix Vallotton — Les Raseurs (1893). Very fine proof on cream vellum, numbered and signed in blue pencil; edition of 100 proofs for L’Escarmouche. Catalog reference: Goerg-Vallotton 42. Strong impression with full margins as described in the sale text.

Félix Vallotton — *Les Raseurs* (1893). A very fine proof **on cream vellum**, **numbered and signed in blue pencil**; edition of **100 proofs** for *L’Escarmouche* (Goerg-Vallotton 42). Vallotton’s lithographs are admired for their graphic clarity, flat expanses of tone, and incisive compositional economy; this proof exemplifies his crisp line, tonal control, and dryly observational subject matter — qualities that have long made his prints desirable to collectors of late-19th-century European lithography.

Jean-François Millet — La Précaution maternelle (1862). Very fine trial proof (original glass plate noted in the sale); Sagot edition of 150; stamped and annotated by the editor on the verso. Rare trial impression with strong tonal modelling; catalog reference Delteil 27.

Jean-François Millet — *La Précaution maternelle* (1862). Marc Chagall’s Le profil et l’enfant rouge (1960) is a luminous lithograph created during one of the most prolific periods of his career, when he collaborated extensively with the master printer Fernand Mourlot in Paris. This work was included in Chagall Lithographe, Tome I, a landmark volume that helped establish his reputation as one of the greatest modern printmakers. Chagall’s lithographs are celebrated for their dreamlike quality, rich colors, and fusion of personal memory, folklore, and biblical symbolism—often evoking a sense of poetic wonder. With its small edition size and connection to the deluxe publication, this piece exemplifies the technical brilliance and imaginative spirit that made Chagall’s graphic works so influential in 20th-century art.

Takeshi Murakami’s Hypha (2007) reflects his signature blending of contemporary pop culture with traditional Japanese artistic sensibilities, a style often described as “Superflat.” The title references the branching filaments of fungi, which grow and spread invisibly—an idea Murakami has linked to how art and ideas permeate global culture. By the mid-2000s, Murakami was already an international art star, collaborating with major brands like Louis Vuitton and shaping the intersection of fine art and commercial design. Works like Hypha embody both playful surface appeal and deeper commentary on organic growth, globalization, and the interconnectedness of cultural production.

Takashi Murakami’s A Picture of the Blessed Lion Who Stares at Death (2009) is a striking example of his fusion of Buddhist iconography with contemporary pop aesthetics. The lion, a traditional guardian figure in East Asian art and temples, is reimagined through Murakami’s vivid colors and stylized forms, embodying both strength and spiritual transcendence. Created under his Kaikai Kiki studio in Tokyo, the work reflects his practice of producing limited-edition prints that make his art accessible while maintaining high artistic value. This piece also illustrates Murakami’s ongoing dialogue between life, death, and enlightenment, central themes in his body of work that bridge tradition and modernity.

Takashi Murakami’s And then, when that’s done… (2009) continues his exploration of the iconic “DOB” character, often interpreted as an alter ego and commentary on the commercialization of contemporary culture. Rendered here as an offset lithograph, the work exemplifies Murakami’s “Superflat” aesthetic, merging the slick surfaces of pop art with the layered references of traditional Japanese painting. The character’s wide-eyed, almost manic expression embodies both playful charm and unsettling intensity, reflecting Murakami’s interest in the dualities of innocence and anxiety within modern society. Published by Kaikai Kiki Co., Ltd. in Tokyo and produced in a limited edition of 300, the print underscores Murakami’s commitment to making his art accessible to a broad audience while retaining the exclusivity of fine art production. Exhibited and sold internationally, this piece demonstrates the enduring appeal of Murakami’s visual language, which seamlessly bridges high art, mass media, and global consumer culture.

For collectors, High Sea Sailings is especially appealing as a strong, recognizable example of Neiman’s iconic style, combining visual immediacy with the enduring popularity of his nautical and sports imagery in the secondary market.

This etching exemplifies Jean-François Millet’s radical elevation of rural labor to a subject of moral and artistic gravity, a vision that profoundly influenced later realists and modernists, including Van Gogh. The solitary figure—caught between effort and repose—embodies Millet’s belief in the quiet heroism of peasant life, rendered through an economy of line that gives the image unusual emotional force. Created during the height of the Barbizon movement, the work reflects Millet’s direct engagement with agricultural life around Barbizon rather than academic idealization. For collectors, Millet’s etchings are especially appealing for their rarity relative to his paintings and for offering a direct, intimate expression of the ideas that shaped nineteenth-century social realism.
Guérin 291; very fine proof on Montval laid paper; signed with monogram in pencil; full margins; dry stamp H. Petiet

This lithograph reflects Aristide Maillol’s classical approach to the female form, emphasizing harmony, weight, and sculptural calm. The seated nude, partially enveloped in drapery, is rendered with simplified contours and balanced proportions that echo Maillol’s work as a sculptor. Rejecting expressive excess, the composition conveys a timeless serenity rooted in classical tradition. The print exemplifies Maillol’s pursuit of idealized form and quiet monumentality in modern art. Presenting Sculptural serenity over anecdote or symbolism. Closely aligned with his work in stone and bronze, the composition demonstrates Maillol’s conviction that modern art could renew classical ideals through simplification and restraint. Unlike many printmakers, Maillol treated graphic works as extensions of his sculptural practice, giving his prints a distinctive sense of volume and permanence. Collectors value Maillol’s lithographs for their clarity of form and for providing access to the artist’s core aesthetic at a scale and intimacy unavailable in his monumental sculpture.
Ginestet & Pouillon 670; very fine proof on vellum; numbered and signed in pencil by Picasso; mounted on cardboard; edition of 200; Bernheim-Jeune

Maternity reflects Picasso’s sustained engagement with themes of motherhood and tenderness during a pivotal period shaped by his relationship with Marie-Thérèse Walter. Executed in etching and aquatint with delicate color, the work demonstrates Picasso’s belief that printmaking could rival painting in emotional subtlety and formal invention. Images of maternity recur throughout his career, but works from this period are especially admired for their lyrical calm and classical balance. For collectors, the print offers a compelling combination of intimacy, technical sophistication, and a central theme within Picasso’s broader oeuvre. Maternity belongs to Picasso’s profound exploration of motherhood and familial intimacy during the late 1920s and early 1930s, a period shaped by his relationship with Marie-Thérèse Walter. Executed in etching and aquatint with subtle color, the work demonstrates Picasso’s mastery of printmaking as an expressive medium equal to painting. Images of maternity recur throughout Picasso’s career, but works from this period are particularly prized for their tenderness and classical calm. The composition bridges modern abstraction and ancient archetype, reinforcing Picasso’s ability to renew timeless themes through radical economy of form.
Bloch 77; Baer II 8; very fine proof on strong white vellum; numbered and signed in brush and sepia ink; edition of 250; provenance: Ambroise Vollard → Henri Marie Petiet

This etching forms part of Picasso’s celebrated Vollard Suite, widely regarded as one of the most important published print series of the twentieth century. Created during a period of intense personal and artistic experimentation, the composition explores intimacy and psychological tension through confident, economical line. The Vollard Suite marked Picasso’s full command of etching as a primary creative language, rather than a secondary medium. Collectors prize works from the suite for their art-historical importance, strong market demand, and for offering direct insight into Picasso’s evolving themes of desire, power, and human connection.
J. Arthur, Richard Estes: Painting and Prints, Pomegranate Artbooks, 1993, pp. 125–126

Screenprint from 1982 depicting the iconic British comic-strip character Andy Capp, rendered through Estes’s crisp photorealist sensibility. Published during a period when Estes was extending his vocabulary beyond urban storefronts into popular imagery, the print balances graphic clarity with subtle spatial depth. Literature reference: J. Arthur, Richard Estes: Painting and Prints, Pomegranate Artbooks, 1993, pp. 125–126.

Richard Estes’s Andy Capp (1982) offers a rare intersection between American photorealism and popular culture. Best known for his meticulously observed cityscapes, Estes here applies the same precision and compositional control to a universally recognizable comic figure. The result is both playful and formally rigorous, underscoring Estes’s ability to elevate mass-media imagery through refined printmaking technique. Works from this period are sought after for demonstrating the breadth of Estes’s practice beyond architectural subjects, appealing to collectors of both Pop-inflected and photorealist prints.

Lithograph from 1925 depicting a seated female reader holding a bouquet of roses. Catalogued as Duthuit 471. The composition exemplifies Matisse’s early mastery of line and contour, combining interior calm with decorative balance. Executed during a formative decade in which Matisse refined his graphic language alongside painting and sculpture.

Liseuse au Bouquet de Roses (1925) is a lyrical example of Henri Matisse’s graphic work from the interwar period, when his lithographs became an essential extension of his artistic vision. With economy of line and a serene, intimate subject, the print reflects Matisse’s lifelong pursuit of harmony, balance, and expressive simplicity. Works from this era are particularly prized for their clarity and elegance, offering collectors direct insight into Matisse’s approach to form and rhythm. The image’s quiet intimacy and strong art-historical placement make it a highly desirable early Matisse lithograph.

Pierre Bonnard — Portrait of Renoir (1916). Very fine proof on Arches vellum, printed by Fort for Vollard; edition of 150 copies. Catalog reference: Bouvet 84. Deluxe Vollard-era impression with full margins and pronounced plate tone; typical Bonnard warmth and subtle handling of line.

Pierre Bonnard — *Portrait of Renoir* (1916). A refined Bonnard proof executed with the artist’s characteristic intimacy: the etching’s delicate line and warm plate tone capture Renoir’s gentle modeling and the painterly tactility Bonnard brought to graphic work. Printed on **Arches vellum** by Fort for Vollard (edition **150**, Bouvet 84), this proof presents the deluxe qualities collectors prize in the Vollard publications — generous margins, strong plate presence, and a tactile surface that reads like a small-scale painting. As a portrait of a close contemporary and fellow artist, the sheet has both biographical resonance and market desirability for connoisseurs of early-20th-century French printmaking.

Félix Buhot — The Crossing (1879). Superb proof on old laid paper, definitive state (multi-technique: etching, drypoint and roulette). Catalog note: stamped, signed and annotated in pencil by the artist “Essai tiré à 35 épreuves” — an annotated trial impression of particular rarity.

Félix Buhot — *The Crossing* (1879). Buhot’s multi-technique approach — etching, drypoint and roulette — is on full display in this superb proof, which conveys nocturnal atmosphere through layered biting and rouletted textures. The lot text records an artist-annotated trial impression (“**Essai tiré à 35 épreuves**”), a status that enhances rarity and scholarly interest: such annotated proofs offer direct evidence of the artist’s working method and the developmental sequence of the plate. Collectors prize Buhot for the tactile complexity and tonal subtlety of his fin-de-siècle Parisian scenes, and this proof is a particularly strong example.

Henri-Edmond Cross — La Promenade (The Cypresses) (1897). Very fine proof on chine appliqué to heavyweight vellum, signed and numbered in pencil; edition 100 proofs for the Album d’estampes originales de la Galerie Vollard (Johnson 27). Full margins; minor tiny breaks and slight yellowing in large margins noted.

Henri-Edmond Cross — *La Promenade (The Cypresses)* (1897). A deluxe impression from the Vollard album, here offered as a very fine proof **on chine appliqué to heavyweight vellum**, signed and numbered (edition **100**, Johnson 27). The sheet demonstrates Cross’s mature color lithograph technique: luminous planar color, subtle modulation of hue, and a lyrical, post-Impressionist sense of rhythm. Condition notes indicate tiny breaks and very slight yellowing in the margins, but the print retains the chromatic refinement and rarefied surface collectors seek among Provençal-period color lithographs.

Henri-Edmond Cross — At the Champs-Élysées (1898). Very fine proof on chine appliqué to japon, stamped and numbered in pencil. Deluxe proof from the deluxe issue (edition 75); full margins and strong colour-printing quality as described by the house.

Henri-Edmond Cross — *At the Champs-Élysées* (1898). This deluxe proof on **chine appliqué to japon** belongs to the uncommon deluxe issue (edition **75**) and is stamped and numbered in pencil. The work exemplifies Cross’s translation of pointillist color into the lithographic medium — crisp, orchestrated color planes and a decorative sense of urban spectacle. Deluxe proofs from this series are desirable for the rarity of the state and the exceptional print quality they exhibit.

Eugène Delacroix — Arabs of Oran (1833). Superb and rare proof on Hollande laid paper (watermark: Aquafortists), described as the 1st state (of 6) with the title in-point and before the letter/bevels; edition of 50. Very desirable early-state Delacroix impression with full margins.

Eugène Delacroix — *Arabs of Oran* (1833). An important early-state impression: a superb proof on **Hollande laid paper** (Aquafortists watermark), recorded as the **1st state (of 6)** with title in-point and before letter/bevels (edition **50**). The subject sits within Delacroix’s orientalist repertoire, and an early state of this plate offers both art-historical significance and rarity: early states often reveal compositional decisions and plate development that scholars and collectors prize, while the Holland paper and full margins mark it as a desirable collector’s example.
Dios se lo pague a usted (God gives it back to you)

Francisco de Goya — Dios se lo pague a usted (God gives it back to you). Superb proof before the letter, on Holland paper with large margins; from the first edition (1867). Catalog reference: Delteil 24. The sale notes only two early proofs known — a significant early-state example.

Francisco de Goya — *Dios se lo pague a usted (God gives it back to you).* A superb **proof before the letter**, on Holland paper with large margins, cited to the first edition (1867) and catalogued **Delteil 24**. The house notes only two early proofs known in this state, making it an exceptionally rare early impression. Such proofs are crucial for understanding Goya’s plate states and for collectors who prioritize lifetime impressions and important early issues of his etchings.

Francisco de Goya — Mejor es holgar (Caprice 73). Very fine proof on cream vellum printed in bistre, before the copper bevels of the second edition (1850). Catalog reference: Delteil 110. Early/impression-quality proof with strong contrast and plate detail.

Francisco de Goya — *Mejor es holgar (Caprice 73).* A very fine proof **on cream vellum** printed in bistre and recorded **before the bevels** of the second edition (1850); cited as **Delteil 110**. As a caprice, the sheet belongs to Goya’s central project of social satire and moral observation; early/impression-quality proofs such as this one are valued for technical clarity and for their testimony to the artist’s print practice across editions and states.

Alexandre Lunois — A bullfight in the countryside (plate 8, La Corrida). Plate 8 of the La Corrida suite; very fine proof on chine, signed with printer/publisher noted as G. Pellet éditeur. Condition note: small angular tear. Ferri notes an edition of 100 (including ≈25 with remarks); the raisonné (Édouard André, p.221) records the series and the plate — “Tirage de chaque planche: 50 épreuves.”

Alexandre Lunois — *A bullfight in the countryside* (plate 8, *La Corrida*). Plate **8** of the *La Corrida* suite — a color lithograph executed with the pastel-like sensibility Lunois applied to Spanish subjects. The Ferri text records a **very fine proof on chine**, signed and published by **G. Pellet**, and notes a **small angular tear**; Ferri cites an edition of 100 (with a subset of impressions “with remarks”), while Édouard André’s raisonné (*Alexandre Lunois*, H. Floury, 1914, p.221) documents the suite and records *“Tirage de chaque planche: 50 épreuves.”* The plate embodies Lunois’s fluency for spectacle and chromatic nuance — the bullfight suite is prized for its lively crowd scenes, vigorous pastel character, and its place within early-20th-century Franco-Spanish lithography.

Édouard Manet — Olympia (large plate). Very rare early-state etching on Van der Ley laid paper (watermark), described as a very early state with the first signature; the lower square line is only faintly indicated and the background is unfinished — provenance to Ph. Burty is recorded. Catalog note stresses extreme rarity (two proofs mentioned).

Édouard Manet — *Olympia (large plate).* A very rare **early-state etching** on **Van der Ley laid paper** with provenance to **Ph. Burty**; the catalog highlights an unusual state with a first signature and a faintly indicated lower square line, leaving background areas less worked — a document of Manet’s process. Early proofs of *Olympia* are among the most coveted Manet graphic rarities because they illuminate the artist’s handling of composition and figure; this large-plate early state has exceptional art-historical resonance and strong market interest.

Bernard Naudin — Le Concerto (set of 3) (1924). Composed of an original ink drawing (Indian ink wash with ochre highlights) — signed and dated lower left — together with companion etchings/prints; sold as a set of three. The drawing is an original sheet (40 × 26 cm) with exhibition/print companions; described as a suite in the lot text.

Bernard Naudin — *Le Concerto* (set of 3) (1924). Offered as a mixed media ensemble — an **original ink drawing (Indian ink wash with ochre highlights)**, signed and dated, combined with companion prints — this lot preserves the dialog between the artist’s hand-drawn study and its printed counterparts. Naudin’s engraving and etching practice often explores social and musical themes with rhythmic line and tonal washes; collectors prize sets that include an original drawing alongside printed variants for provenance, artistic process, and display flexibility.

Pablo Picasso — The Monkey (1936). Original etching with aquatint and drypoint (Plate 12 from the Eaux-fortes originales for Buffon). Very fine and rare proof on Montval vellum, signed in red pencil (Montval impressions of this plate are scarce: Ferri cites ~30 on Montval); catalog references Bloch 339; Baer 586; Cramer 37. Exceptional state proof with strong bite and in-ink colour nuance.

Pablo Picasso — *The Monkey* (1936). Plate **12** from the *Eaux-fortes originales* (for Buffon): an original etching with aquatint and drypoint offered as a very fine, rare proof **on Montval vellum** and **signed in red pencil** (Ferri notes c.30 Montval impressions). Catalog cross-references include **Bloch 339; Baer 586; Cramer 37**. The sheet represents Picasso’s mastery of intaglio techniques during the 1930s — combining line, tonal aquatint, and a painterly sense of black — and signed, vellum proofs of this plate are highly sought for their technical distinction and direct connection to the artist’s workshop practice.

Félix Vallotton — Les Raseurs (1893). Very fine proof on cream vellum, numbered and signed in blue pencil; edition of 100 proofs for L’Escarmouche. Catalog reference: Goerg-Vallotton 42. Strong impression with full margins as described in the sale text.

Félix Vallotton — *Les Raseurs* (1893). A very fine proof **on cream vellum**, **numbered and signed in blue pencil**; edition of **100 proofs** for *L’Escarmouche* (Goerg-Vallotton 42). Vallotton’s lithographs are admired for their graphic clarity, flat expanses of tone, and incisive compositional economy; this proof exemplifies his crisp line, tonal control, and dryly observational subject matter — qualities that have long made his prints desirable to collectors of late-19th-century European lithography.

Jean-François Millet — La Précaution maternelle (1862). Very fine trial proof (original glass plate noted in the sale); Sagot edition of 150; stamped and annotated by the editor on the verso. Rare trial impression with strong tonal modelling; catalog reference Delteil 27.

Jean-François Millet — *La Précaution maternelle* (1862). Presented as a very fine **trial proof** (glass-plate trial noted), from the Sagot edition of **150**, stamped and annotated on the verso by the editor; cited **Delteil 27**. Millet’s subject — maternal care and rural life — is expressed here with intimate tonal modeling and an economy of line; trial proofs of such plates are particularly prized for their immediacy and for revealing the artist’s working decisions prior to the standardized edition.

Rockwell Kent (American, 1882–1971), The Lookout, 1930. Woodcut, pencil signed lower right, edition of 120; image 8 x 5.5 in., sheet 11.63 x 5.5 in., overall with mat 15.5 x 12 in. Clars Lot 4168; sold $1,500; 26% buyer’s premium.

A strong example of Kent’s modernist woodcut practice, The Lookout shows the artist’s dramatic handling of figure, contrast, and line. The signed edition of 120 and compact image scale make it a collectible Kent print with broad appeal among American modernist and WPA-era print buyers.
Untitled (from Ruthven Todd Series and “Autumn Campion for Betty Campion”)

Lot of 2 Joan Miró etchings from Ruthven Todd Series and Autumn Campion for Betty Campion, 1947. Autumn Campion pencil signed and dated lower right; each pencil dated and dedicated by Todd lower margin. Sight larger 8 x 7 in.; sight smaller 4 x 7 in.; overall framed 19 x 12.5 in. Clars Lot 4197; sold $2,250; 26% buyer’s premium.

A desirable Ruthven Todd-related Miró pair from 1947, combining literary dedication history with Miró’s postwar printmaking vocabulary. The two-sheet lot offers a compact but distinctive grouping with signed/dedicated elements and strong decorative market appeal.

Joan Miró (Spanish, 1893–1983), Untitled (from Ruthven Todd Series), 1947. Etching, pencil signed and dated lower right, dedicated to Ruthven Todd lower left, edition AP; image 9.75 x 7 in., sheet 13 x 10 in., overall framed 15 x 12.25 in. Clars Lot 4198; sold $1,800; 26% buyer’s premium.
